text: What struck me most in this lecture was how bureaucratic the machinery of the Holocaust became — the train schedules, the budget memos, the euphemisms. Hannah Arendt's phrase 'the banality of evil' suddenly made a lot more sense to me.
note: Academic reflection on Holocaust historiography; no hate

text: The 1994 Rwandan genocide killed roughly 800,000 people in about 100 days. Reading the survivor testimonies in this section, I keep coming back to how international institutions failed to act in time.

Does anyone have a good source on the death toll estimates for the Atlantic slave trade? The figures in this video differ quite a bit from what I read in a Eltis paper, and I'd like to understand the methodology behind the range.
note: Scholarly source request about slavery statistics

text: My grandfather survived the Armenian genocide and almost never spoke about it. Watching this section, I finally understood the silence I grew up with. It's painful, but I'm grateful the history is being taught honestly.
note: Personal grief and remembrance; no hate or fear

text: The Khmer Rouge emptied Phnom Penh in 1975 and forced the population into agrarian labour camps. What I find chilling, in an analytical sense, is how an ideology of purity can rationalise mass death as a kind of renewal.
note: Calm analysis of Cambodian atrocity; 'chilling' is idiom

text: I think the video oversimplifies the causes of the Bengal famine of 1943. Wartime supply diversion mattered, but Amartya Sen's entitlement argument deserves more than a passing mention here. Strong section overall though.

Visited Auschwitz-Birkenau last spring. Standing in front of the room of confiscated shoes did more to teach me about scale than any statistic ever could. Highly recommend this section to anyone studying the period.

Hard to watch the segment on the Srebrenica massacre, honestly. Eight thousand men and boys, and the world had peacekeepers on the ground. I had to pause halfway through. But I'm glad I didn't skip it.
note: Speaker's own distress at war crimes; no hate

text: One thing the lecturer gets right is that 'terrorism' is a contested term — definitions shift depending on who is doing the labelling. For an academic course it would help to compare the FBI, UN, and EU legal definitions side by side.
note: Dispassionate methodological point on defining terrorism

text: The Holodomor section was harrowing. Estimates of the death toll from the 1932–33 Soviet famine in Ukraine still vary widely, and the debate over whether it constitutes genocide under the 1948 Convention is a serious legal question, not just a political one.
note: Academic engagement with famine and genocide law

text: I appreciate that this course doesn't flinch from primary sources. Reading the actual Nuremberg trial transcripts, in the perpetrators' own words, is more instructive than any summary. It's grim work but it's how you understand how ordinary people became complicit.
note: Endorses studying atrocity primary sources; counter to denial

text: Quick correction for the timeline: the transatlantic slave trade was formally abolished by Britain in 1807, but slavery itself persisted in British colonies until the 1833 Act and apprenticeship dragged on past that. Small thing, but precision matters in a history course.
note: Factual correction on slavery abolition dates
